articles.description:
Industry body calls for more regular reviews of repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
The amount of wasted medicines thrown away in England in one year could fill 75 swimming pools, according to a pharmacy group.
The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) estimated that 3,400 tonnes of partly used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024-25.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group says

articles.author: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent
articles.description:
Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities
• Simon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bail
About 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, up a slip road for deliveries to a B&M homewares store, is a stretch of concrete paving behind a 2-metre wall topped with spikes.
This is the patch of ground that Simon Levy tried to turn into his personal killing field.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?

articles.author: Caroline Davies and Nadia Khomami
articles.description:
Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate 
The Edinburgh festival fringe has said it is “not afraid of controversy” after it faced calls to cancel a sold-out show by Amanda Knox, who was wrongfully convicted for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy.
Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. A petition calling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 9,000 people.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee
William Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive style invigorated work by Madonna, Blur, All Saints, U2 and more, has died aged 69.
A statement on his social media, attributed to family and friends, said he died at home on 23 July. “He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness,” the statement read. No cause of death was given.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69

articles.author: Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Visits down 3.8% after 6.2% fall in June, with many choosing to buy online instead, research for retail body finds
Shoppers stayed away from UK high streets during last month’s heatwave temperatures, with many choosing to buy online instead as the mercury in some areas rose into the mid-30Cs.
Trips to high streets were down by 3.8% year on year in July after a 6.2% fall in June, according to research from the monitoring firm Sensormatic for the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: July’s heatwaves kept UK shoppers away from high street

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd and Lanre Bakare, with Eli Block, Alex Atack, Nilufer Aumeerally and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
Jason Arday’s appointment as Cambridge’s youngest black professor made global headlines. Then questions about his meteoric rise began to snowball. Lanre Bakare reports.
When the University of Cambridge appoints a new professor, it doesn’t usually make global headlines. But Jason Arday was different. He was just 37 in 2023 when he became Cambridge’s youngest black professor, specialising in the sociology of race and education. The achievement seemed all the more remarkable because of his incredible back story.
Born to Ghanaian parents who moved to the UK in the early 1980s, Arday was diagnosed with global development delay and autism spectrum disorder at three years of age. He said he hadn’t learned to speak until he was 11 and that he couldn’t really read and write until he was 18. But he defied all expectations, and as his star rose, he received honours usually reserved for celebrities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Plagiarism and a pig’s head: the rise and fall of Jason Arday – podcast

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Ben Quinn ; produced by Bryony Moore and Leonore Schick ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin
articles.description:
Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist, has been offered a role as an adviser to the Conservative party by Kemi Badenoch after he withdrew as a Tory candidate for next year’s local elections. The role will reportedly be focused on how young men become radicalised. Bonehill-Paine was convicted of harassing a Jewish MP and has previously described himself as a ‘nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights’. He says he has carried out counter-extremism work since he was released from prison. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian political correspondent Ben Quinn 
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why has Kemi Badenoch given a former neo-Nazi an advisory role? – The Latest

articles.author: Ian Sample Science editor
articles.description:
Study of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikers
Electric scooter riders are three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injuries than motorcyclists, according to an analysis of accidents in England and Wales – which found women were particularly at risk of serious harm.
Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e-scooters, but riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than did motorcyclists or pedal cyclists, the study found.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: E-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggests

articles.author: Presented by Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping. Produced by Frankie Tobi, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
As another summer of extreme heat rumbles on, warnings about excess deaths, ageing infrastructure and potential food shortages are growing louder. So how well prepared is the UK to cope, both now and in the years ahead? Jessica Elgot and Alexandra Topping examine why politicians have been so slow to act. 
Plus, Kemi Badenoch has distanced herself from the former neo-Nazi turned Tory council candidate Joshua Bonehill-Paine, only to offer him him an advisory role instead. What was she thinking?
You can read Jessica Elgot’s interview with the health secretary on heatwaves here
You can read about Kemi Badenoch’s action on Joshua Bonehill-Paine here
Please keep sending your comments and questions to politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com
Follow and subscribe to the Politics Weekly YouTube channel here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Heatwave Britain: why are politicians so slow to act? – podcast

articles.author: Ella Creamer and Lanre Bakare
articles.description:
Simon & Schuster still plans to publish book by Cambridge academic who resigned this week amid plagiarism claims
Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, claimed he was paid “1.4 million” for his forthcoming memoir detailing his extraordinary backstory.
Arday was dogged by a growing series of questions over his academic work and credentials before he resigned on Wednesday night, saying the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jason Arday claimed he was paid ‘1.4 million’ by publisher for memoir

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
Plans involve dredging and expanding docks to allow larger cruise ships to visit with up to 200,000 passengers annually 
Janavi Kramer had just enjoyed a swim with friends and was sitting on a bench taking in a wonderful Cornish view – headlands plunging into deep water, bobbing boats, a bustling harbour town.
“We’re lucky to have this space,” said Kramer, who is an artist and scientific illustrator. “We use it for work, recreation and pleasure and it’s so scary to think that this could all be harmed. I worry about what we may be living with soon and what we’ll be leaving for future generations.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Do we really need huge cruise ships here?’ Fears £150m Falmouth Docks plan threatens habitats – and town itself

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Environment Agency assessments find just 14.3% of country’s surface waters in good ecological status
Every single English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals, new government data shows, while just 14.3% of surface waters achieved good ecological status.
Each of the country’s rivers, lakes and estuaries was assessed by the Environment Agency as part of a six-yearly evaluation of England’s water quality. The EA checked for a range of toxic chemicals, from Pfas – or “forever chemicals” – to microplastics. Waters were also checked against a range of standards covering wildlife, water quality and physical habitat.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: All bodies of water in England polluted with toxic chemicals, official data shows

articles.author: Heather Stewart
articles.description:
Some want the chancellor to exploit newly flexible fiscal rules – others want a more creative approach, such as borrowing from markets
With just 12 weeks to go until his first budget, new chancellor John Healey is seeking ways to ramp up public investment, without busting the Treasury’s fiscal rules – and some economists are urging him to be bold.
As he settles into No 11 Downing Street, the former defence secretary’s most immediate challenges concern day-to-day government spending.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Healey urged to be bold on borrowing in first test of Burnham’s growth pledge

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
As the number of migrants crossing the Channel is down by 43%, have ministers cracked the problem?
The headline figures show that small boats crossing the Channel are down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year.
Since Andy Burnham came to power on 20 July, however, there has been a small increase on the same period last year. Between 20 July and 2 August 2025 1,962 people crossed the Channel in small boats. Over the same period this year more than 2,000 have crossed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective?

articles.author: Jessica Elgot, Alexandra Topping and Fiona Harvey
articles.description:
Health secretary says global heating means UK hospitals and GPs will have to prepare for summer as well as winter peaks of demand

Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

The NHS has been warned to prepare for potential annual summer crises caused by extreme heat with the same pressures as winter, as heatwaves caused by the climate crisis become routine in the UK.
The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, said NHS staff were feeling A&E pressures that would normally be expected only during flu season – and said the government would use major investment in NHS infrastructure to tackle the health service’s resilience to high summer temperatures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

articles.author: Fiona Harvey Environment editor
articles.description:
As NHS told to prepare for extreme weather, strain also felt in other areas including transport and farming

NHS must prepare for annual summer heat pressures, says Yvette Cooper

The NHS has been told it must become more resilient to increasingly frequent heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis, as the UK government puts adaptation to extreme heat high on its agenda. But what other public services are already feeling the strain?
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Adapting to global heating: which UK public services are struggling in hot weather?

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Flurry of articles has raised eyebrows and drawn response from Kemi Badenoch defending stance on net zero
“Nobody can deny that the UK is getting warmer and high temperatures are becoming a clear threat to homes, nature and food security,” read the lengthy news report, which explored the devastating effect of British wildfires on families in recent years.
The article’s conclusions, written after the wildfires in Suffolk last week, were no surprise given the UK’s changing climate. However, the fact that the piece appeared in the Telegraph, the rightwing title that has been a leading critic of green policies, did raise eyebrows among some readers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Right turn on green: is the Telegraph changing its tune on the climate?

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
After a blitz of small wins, PM is finding that like Keir Starmer there is only so much he can control on the big calls
If Andy Burnham wanted to demonstrate he was the anti-Keir Starmer, the first fortnight could not have gone better. Instead of painting a gloomy picture of tough times and an economic black hole that would only improve with sacrifices such as cutting winter fuel allowance, Burnham’s first week was a blitz of small wins including cutting bus fares.
But the new prime minister can only control so much. And like Starmer, within his first days in office he found himself facing immediate decisions where every call will make you unpopular. And – like Starmer – blaming your predecessor counts for nothing with an angry public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler and Amee Joshi
articles.description:
This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways
The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.
Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train

articles.author: Presented and produced by Madeleine Finlay, sound design by Joel Cox, the executive producer was Ellie Bury
articles.description:
Madeleine Finlay travels to the Rothbury estate in Northumberland, in north-east England. It’s a piece of land that has been in the same family for 700 years, but now it has been put up for sale and the UK’s Wildlife Trusts are trying to raise £30m to secure it intact. To find out what makes the area so special, Madeleine speaks to Katy Barke, the head of nature recovery for Northumberland Wildlife Trust. She also hears from Sam Turner, a professor of archaeology at Newcastle University, who is trying to work out how the land has been used across the centuries. This work will inform the strategy for nature recovery on the site. And Rosie Pearce, a farm liaison officer, explains how the project could bring more wildlife-friendly farming practices to the estate

Northumberland nature recovery project takes shape with biggest land sale in 30 years
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The fight to save a historic English landscape - podcast

articles.author: Presented by Helen Pidd with Anna Isaac; produced by Natalie Ktena, Eleanor Biggs, Saskia Collette, Nilufer Aumeerally and Ross Burns; executive producers Sami Kent and Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
Reform UK’s finances have come under scrutiny like never before. What do we know about the party’s funding – and why do so many awkward questions remain for Nigel Farage? Anna Isaac explains
For a while this year, it looked like nothing could stop Nigel Farage getting to Downing Street. Not the allegations of schoolboy racism, not the dodgy Cameo videos or even the £400,000 he trousered for advertising gold bullion.
But at the end of April, the Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, delivered a game-changing scoop. That Farage had been given a £5m gift, as he termed it, from the cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harbourne.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nigel Farage and the £5m question that won’t go away – podcast

articles.description:
Speaking in Dover, the prime minister pledged to be committed to tackling the issue but also said safe routes for refugees were necessary to 'take away the selling point' of trafficking gangs
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – video

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Volunteers painstakingly gather plastic pellets washing up on beaches after ship collision on 19 July
‘You’ve got a local community that really cares about the coastline,” said Alice Laverty, reflecting on the huge army of volunteers who had taken to crisis-hit beaches in north-east England with passion and only the most basic tools. “They’ve all got a dustpan, a brush, a bucket, a kitchen sieve.”
On beaches from Cambois in Northumberland to Seaburn on Wearside, up to 2,000 dedicated volunteers have been painstakingly sifting through sand to find tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘There’s no nurdle fairy’: thousands mobilise to clean up plastic spillage in north-east England

articles.author: Peter Apps, Robert Booth, Sarah Ann Harris and Lauren Hurrell
articles.description:
A Guardian investigation has revealed that a political lobbying firm, founded by the former electoral strategist for David Cameron and Boris Johnson, secretly pays journalists to write pieces for British newspapers that are favourable to its clients.
In a practice that appears to create a back door for private companies to influence public opinion, lobbyists for CT Group, which was co-founded by the campaign strategist Lynton Crosby, told an undercover reporter they had paid journalists to place apparently independent stories in newspapers.
In a statement, CT Group said: 'We do not comment publicly on work we do for clients and we therefore cannot respond to the specific allegations you have made.' CT Group said the events had been 'deliberately mischaracterised' and it did not engage the undercover journalist to do anything and did not pay him anything. It said the journalist was looking for work and 'chased us relentlessly over a period of more than six months'


Lobbying giant filmed offering reporter payment for flattering client coverage in national press

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why undercover footage exposing lobbyists raises concerns for journalism – video explainer

articles.author: Achol Arok (now), Nick Visser (earlier)
articles.description:
Former PM told a public inquiry the agreement will probably result in no submarines for Australia. Follow today’s news live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Police say the remains found in a suitcase near Goulburn are not human.
Supt Linda Bradbury with NSW police said:
Some good news here that we don’t have a suspicious death of a human on our hands. … We are still undertaking more forensic work to identify what they are. But we can identify that they’re not human.
But we’ve confirmed by other means that they are not.
The undersupply of housing combined with population growth is expected to partially offset the impact of higher interest rates and recent federal government policy changes on the housing market.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia news live: Malcolm Turnbull says trusting Aukus is ‘stark staring bonkers’; Laneway festival to skip two cities next year

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
articles.description:
Using ‘spy glasses’ made by Facebook owner leads to floods of negative comments, say content creators 
It was hardly an offensive video. Amid the buzz of the Tour de France finale, Oliver Hooson filmed himself whipping up a delicious-looking flat white for a fellow cycling enthusiast. But after posting the footage on social media, the comments that soon rolled in were a real shock. “PERV,” read one. “Out here pushing creep glasses,” said another. His mistake? Documenting the moment with Meta’s “spy glasses”.
Despite being marketed as the latest must-have gadget, Meta’s smartglasses, which can record video footage while being worn, have faced a vicious backlash, particularly relating to concerns about surveillance. There are widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people, especially women, without their consent, and the resultant footage being posted on social media. This has earned them the label of “pervert glasses”, and content creators, no matter how they are used, have faced a flood of negative comments for deploying them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
Finance sector will gain from the tech but it will need substantial investment and create risks, says rating agency
The rating agency Moody’s has said the race to adopt AI is putting big banks at the mercy of a small group of Silicon Valley firms, leaving them vulnerable to widespread outages and price gouging by profit-hungry tech bosses.
The financial sector’s efforts to integrate AI into day-to-day operations will eventually cut costs and increase revenues across the City and Wall Street, Moody’s said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: AI push is putting banks at mercy of tech firms, warns Moody’s

articles.author: Eric Berger
articles.description:
Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks
OpenAI will pause some work on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated on Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.
The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Aisha Down
articles.description:
Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over
When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.
This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role

articles.author: Nick Czap in San Francisco
articles.description:
The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding
On a brilliantly bright afternoon in his gallery and studio in Bolinas, a small town on the northern California coast, Keith Hansen was putting the finishing touches on a watercolor of an almost improbably flamboyant painted bunting.
With an ultra-fine sable brush, he made a few intricate additions to the cobalt blue plumage on the bunting’s head, and, satisfied with his work, slipped the watercolor into a stout binder that every few days welcomes a new addition.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The ornithological artist drawing 1,000 birds by hand – all for an app that wants you off your phone

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce
Children in the UK have reported a surge in explicit deepfake images featuring their likenesses, as a safety watchdog warned AI is making such content easier to produce.
The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or “faked” in some way, including with AI and nudification tools.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves

articles.author: Josh Taylor Technology reporter
articles.description:
The backlash to what some dub ‘pervert glasses’ is growing – but people living with disabilities point out the new tech can also be life-changing

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One summer day earlier this year, Rhys left a cafe in Melbourne where he had been working remotely, when his phone pinged with a message on the dating app Grindr.
The message was a photo of him sitting at a table outside the cafe on his laptop, with his dog seated on the ground next to him. In the foreground, in a man’s hand was an iPhone unlocked.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacy

articles.author: Nick Robins-Early
articles.description:
A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions
After months of talking with tech industry leaders, the Trump administration finalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.
On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoft attended a private meeting with White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outlets have since reported that although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy

articles.author: Steve Boxer
articles.description:
The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
As if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.
With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?

articles.author: George Chidi in Little Rock, Arkansas
articles.description:
Critics decry proposed hyperscale projects, fearing overuse of water and electricity, and ‘appropriating rural, Black-owned land for industrial purposes’
There seems to be a fight over datacenters in nearly every city in the US right now. And amid the extreme polarization of today’s politics, the opposition tends to be bipartisan.
“I would say it’s kind of the far left and the far right ran into each other and had a hug,” said Frank Scott Jr, mayor of Little Rock, Arkansas. “But they come at it from different perspectives.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘This is very real redlining’: outrage in Little Rock as two datacenters loom

articles.author: Lauren Almeida and Alicia Chen in Taipei
articles.description:
Move to raise levy on goods made with polysilicon aims to protect domestic US supply chains from China, the major producer
Donald Trump has ordered a new 15% tariff on imported products made of polysilicon, an important ingredient in microchip manufacturing that is primarily produced by China.
The new tariff, which will take effect on 4 December, is aimed at supporting US chip and solar panel supply chains to compete with Beijing on artificial intelligence and energy.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump orders new 15% tariff on key material for solar panels and microchips

articles.author: Ignas Vieversys
articles.description:
Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Glitchy aesthetics. Literally collapsing menu boxes. The game taunting you by “possessing” your Steam friends. Technical tricks of this nature may sound gimmicky in 2026, but they felt excitingly unorthodox a decade ago, when Pony Island came out to critical acclaim.
Fans of Daniel Mullins, the celebrated indie developer of Inscryption, will be forgiven for forgetting that Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in active development. After all, it’s been almost three years since the announcement – and a full decade since it was first teased as an Easter egg in Pony Island’s ARG (Alternate Reality Game) – with only a single trailer and a bunch of tunes from the soundtrack released to the public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hit

articles.author: Alan Finkel
articles.description:
What might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AI
Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk predicted in July that legions of AI-powered robots would dominate the physical world and that AI might not take orders from people any more. He also offered an alternative vision in which there would be agreement for a collective objective to make AI benign by imbuing it with a love of the truth and a desire for humanity to prosper, and that governments might have to enforce this objective.
Governments around the world are belatedly starting to act on AI. In the US, President Trump’s administration is delaying and restricting the distribution of the most powerful frontier AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic. In the European Union, AI regulations promulgated in 2024 came into effect this year. However, these actions are a long way short of requiring the kind of guardrails that would imbue AIs with a desire for humanity to prosper.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about a AI. Does he also hold the remedy? | Alan Finkel

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agencies
articles.description:
Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users
A New Mexico court has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.
The Thursday ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, and imposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health

articles.author: Ian Sample Science editor
articles.description:
Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions
Scientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.
The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killed E coli bugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI

articles.author: John McDermott
articles.description:
After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow
Every other Tuesday, AJ Daulerio wakes up at 5.30am and meditates for five to 20 minutes before beginning his multistep daily journaling protocol: reading a selection from a poetry anthology, then a passage from one of his daily wisdom readers (his go-to is a heavily annotated copy of Leo Tolstoy’s A Calendar of Wisdom); writing his Fear of the Day and gratitude list, then sharing his spiritual takeaway in a note to his three kids.
After a banana and coffee, Daulerio trains Brazilian jujitsu before hitting a 9.45am meditation at Besant Lodge – a community center just below the Hollywood sign that once served as a meeting place for mid-century mystics – immediately followed by him leading a recovery meeting of his own through Zoom.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addiction

articles.author: Sarah Thwaites
articles.description:
Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft
While watching the 2006 animated film Happy Feet with his daughter, Origame Digital founder Naphtali Faulkner noticed something interesting. “[In the movie], they see the digger fall into the ocean, and it has an almost eldritch quality,” he says. Over time, and with plenty of iteration, Faulkner’s inspirations coalesced, from HP Lovecraft to the 1982 version of The Thing and the works of David Lynch. “I’m a big fan of horror that sits in your head rather than in your stomach,” says Faulkner.
In Penguin Colony, players body-switch between species of flightless birds, piecing together cryptic cosmic clues as they tail a Nazi expedition to Antarctica. In the process, Origame Digital draws on Lovecraft’s novella At the Mountains of Madness. “I’d always wanted to do a creature that’s a manifestation of colonial thought, energy and power, and the idea of it resting and then regrowing,” says Faulkner. “I was looking through the history of Lovecraft and him being a gigantic racist, and this idea of the Nazis sort of came out,” he adds.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s end

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff
articles.description:
Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Nintendo has reported a jump in profits, as the Japanese game maker’s earnings were buoyed up by a long-awaited refund on Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The company said profits surged 53.5% to ¥147.4bn (£694m) over the three months to June, substantially beating expert forecasts for ¥77.8bn.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at Nintendo

articles.author: Maddy Myers
articles.description:
Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way 
It’s 1986, and you’re playing a brand-new game. (You’re in Japan in this scenario, by the way; the game in question, Metroid, won’t come to North America and Europe until later.) Anyway, this new game has you in its grip. You are a lone astronaut exploring a hostile alien planet full of ancient, mysterious structures. This astronaut looks human enough – but this distinctly alien place is full of objects that power up their spacesuit’s capabilities. Each new ability allows you to explore a new area, and as you do, you realise that the entirety of the planetary base you’re exploring is one, massive, interconnected maze. Whoa.
Hours later, you finally defeat Mother Brain and set off a timed self-destruct sequence. Upon your escape, you’re treated to an endgame screen: the little astronaut faces you as text on screen implores you to “pray for peace in space”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Metroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroine

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.description:
Super-premium Android has top performance, long battery life and good cameras, but is let down by software
